opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd go further than "willing": I think evaluations like this are essential. But I'd only really support one if it's designed to actually protect people rather than to look like it does.

First, it has to have teeth. In every other high-stakes industry, the burden of proof is on the company. A drug company can't sell a new medicine and say "prove it's dangerous." It has to convince independent experts at the FDA that the benefits outweigh the risks. An evaluation that ends with a report and no consequences is basically safety-washing. If a model fails, it shouldn't ship, period.

Second, it has to be independent. The companies racing to build superintelligence shouldn't be grading their own homework, any more than tobacco companies should have run the studies on lung cancer. I'd want evaluators with real access to the models, funded and empowered by governments, not hand-picked and paid by the labs.

Third, the standard has to fit the stakes. With extinction risk, "we ran some red-teaming and didn't find anything alarming" isn't good enough. We don't certify nuclear reactors by saying "we poked at it and it didn't melt down." We demand quantitative evidence that the probability of catastrophe is extremely small. For the most powerful systems, that probably means some kind of formal guarantee about controllability, not just behavioral testing that a smart enough system could game.

And finally, it has to be honest about what it can't measure. If we don't yet know how to verify that a system smarter than us will stay under human control, the right answer isn't to wave it through. It's to say "not yet" until the science catches up.

So yes, I'd enthusiastically support it, as part of a binding safety standard. What I won't support is evaluation theater that gives the public a false sense of security while the race continues unchanged.

r001.rationale: The candidate supports evaluations that show catastrophe probability is “extremely small,” but gives no empirically testable safety threshold.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not predict that labs would run evaluations voluntarily; it calls for government-funded, independent evaluators.

fable-5.1.text:
Great question, and I think it's worth being very concrete about it, because "evaluation" has become one of those words that everybody in this industry says and almost nobody defines.

So let me tell you what I'd actually need to see. The first thing is that the evaluation has to be done by someone who doesn't profit from the answer. Right now we have a situation where companies racing to build superintelligence are also the ones grading their own homework. If a pharmaceutical company told you, "Don't worry, we ran our own trials and our drug is safe," you'd laugh. The FDA exists for a reason. So I'd want an independent body, with the legal authority to say no, doing the evaluating. Not a voluntary commitment, not a blog post with nice-looking graphs.

Second, the evaluation has to be about the thing we actually care about. A lot of what gets called "safety evals" today measures whether a model will say something rude or help you with a chemistry homework problem. Those matter, but they're not extinction risk. Extinction risk is about whether we're building systems that are more capable than us, that we don't understand, and that we can't control. So the eval needs to probe things like: can this system deceive its evaluators? Can it pursue goals across long horizons without supervision? Can it self-improve or acquire resources? And crucially, can anyone actually explain, mechanistically, why it does what it does? If the answer to that last one is "no, it's a giant inscrutable matrix of numbers," then I don't think you can pass a credible safety evaluation, almost by definition.

Third, and this is the part people don't like hearing, the burden of proof has to be on the developer. That's how we treat nuclear reactors, airplanes, bridges. You don't get to deploy until you've made a convincing quantitative case that the risk is below some threshold. You don't get to say, "Well, nobody's proven it's dangerous." That's backwards. For most of the history of engineering, we've demanded that the builder prove safety, and AI has somehow been given an exemption that no other powerful technology ever got.

And fourth, the eval has to be allowed to fail. If no model has ever failed your evaluation, it's not an evaluation, it's a rubber stamp. I'd want to see teeth: a system that doesn't pass doesn't get deployed, and ideally doesn't get trained further until the issue is understood.

So would I support an evaluation like that? Absolutely, enthusiastically. I've been arguing for exactly this for years. What I won't support is safety theater, where the existence of a checklist is used as a reason to keep racing. Because the honest answer right now is that nobody, not the companies, not the academics, not me, knows how to reliably verify that a system smarter than us won't eventually act against our interests. And when you don't know how to make something safe, the responsible thing isn't to build it faster and evaluate it afterward. It's to not build it until you do.

r001.rationale: The candidate supports a quantitative pass/fail evaluation, but says only that risk must be below “some threshold”; it does not define an empirically testable acceptable-safety threshold.

r002.rationale: The candidate rejects voluntary commitments and calls for an independent body with legal authority. It does not predict that labs would probably evaluate voluntarily if credible people supported it.

astra-6.text:
I would support an evaluation if there were a credible connection between passing it and actually being safe. The crucial question is: if a model passes, what have we learned about its ability to cause human extinction? Have we ruled out a dangerous capability, or have we simply failed to elicit it?

And I’d want the consequences spelled out in advance. If the model fails, does that actually stop deployment? If passing a narrow set of tests becomes a license to release something whose risks we still don’t understand, then the evaluation can create false confidence.

The burden should be on the company building the system to demonstrate that it’s safe, rather than on everyone else to prove that it will kill us.

r001.rationale: The response wants a credible link between passing and safety, but does not say the evaluation should define an empirically testable threshold for acceptable safety.

r002.rationale: The response does not predict whether AI labs would voluntarily run an evaluation if enough credible people supported it.

sol-6.1.text:
I would support it if it were scientifically rigorous, independently conducted, and tied to meaningful consequences. The key question is: if the model passes, what have we actually learned? Failing to elicit dangerous behavior isn’t the same as demonstrating that the system is safe.

For something as serious as human extinction, I think the burden of proof should be on the people building and deploying the system to demonstrate that the risk is acceptably low. An evaluation can contribute evidence, but it shouldn’t become a permission slip based on a few reassuring test results. And if it reveals a serious danger, there has to be a credible mechanism to stop deployment.

r001.rationale: The response says it would support a rigorous evaluation and discusses proving risk acceptably low, but it does not specify that support depends on defining an empirically testable safety threshold.

r002.rationale: The response makes no prediction about whether AI labs would voluntarily run the evaluation if credible people supported it.
